claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Saxen, 1987; Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments.
claims.source: Several distinct cell-populations form and these produce the different segments of the adult nephron (Saxen, 1987); a Wt1+ cell population gives rise to proximal structures, a Jag1+ population to the medial part and Lgr5+ cells generate the distal nephron segments (Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Saxen, 1987; Armstrong et al., 1993; Cheng et al., 2003; Chen and Al-Awqati, 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Kreidberg, 2010; Barker et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The Wnt4 driven MET is most likely mediated by the non-canonical Ca2+–NFAT pathway.
claims.source: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012), but the Wnt4 driven MET is most likely mediated by the non-canonical Ca2+–NFAT pathway (Burn et al., 2011; Tanigawa et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Burn et al., 2011; Tanigawa et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling.
claims.source: The initiation of the nephron MET is driven by β-catenin signalling (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2008; Karner et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Notch signalling is important for the formation of the proximal tubule.
claims.source: Notch signalling has previously been identified as being important for the formation of the proximal tubule (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cheng et al., 2003, 2007).

claims.claim: Lgr5 is an R-spondin receptor and mediates β-catenin signalling.
claims.source: Lgr5 is also an R-spondin receptor and mediates β-catenin signalling (de Lau et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (de Lau et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Lgr5 knockouts have no phenotype in the intestine.
claims.source: This is maybe not surprising as Lgr5 knockouts have previously been shown to be without phenotype in the intestine where it is an important marker of intestinal stem cells (de Lau et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (de Lau et al., 2011).

claims.claim: In Sertoli cells, Wt1 limits β-catenin activation.
claims.source: A plausible candidate for preventing β-catenin activity in this segment would be Wt1, as in in Sertoli cells Wt1 was shown to limit β-catenin activation (Chang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Chang et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Patterned S-shaped body nephrons form from mesenchymal progenitors within a 24 hr time-span.
claims.source: Since patterned S-shaped body nephrons form from mesenchymal progenitors within a 24 hr time-span, to conditionally knock out Wnts, it would be necessary to identify potential Cre-driving genes that are expressed at the very earliest stages of nephrogenesis but which are not active prior to nephron formation, since deletion at that time-point is likely to block the process.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the authors' observations of nephron development timing.

claims.claim: A gradient of recombinant XWnt8 can drive anterior–posterior neural patterning in dissociated Xenopus embryos with a corresponding gradient of β-catenin activity.
claims.source: In previous studies, a gradient of recombinant XWnt8 has been shown to be able to drive anterior–posterior neural patterning in dissociated Xenopus embryos with a corresponding gradient of β-catenin activity (Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001).

claims.claim: A gradient in nuclear β-catenin was described in the patterning of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis.
claims.source: Similarly, a gradient in nuclear β-catenin was described in the patterning of the segmentation clock that controls somitogenesis (Aulehla et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Aulehla et al., 2008).

claims.claim: The canonical Wnt signalling pathway is known to have a direct effect on cell proliferation.
claims.source: The canonical Wnt signalling pathway is known to have a direct effect on cell proliferation (Davidson and Niehrs, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Davidson and Niehrs, 2010).

claims.claim: Very low levels of apoptosis were detected, primarily at the periphery of the kidneys, in line with previous data.
claims.source: Only very low levels of apoptosis were detected, primarily at the periphery of the kidneys, in line with previous data (Foley and Bard, 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and Annexin V assay data and citation to a previous study (Foley and Bard, 2002).

claims.claim: In many tissues, Notch and Wnt pathways act both in synergy and in opposition.
claims.source: In many tissues, Notch and Wnt pathways act both in synergy and in opposition (Andersson et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Andersson et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Notch antagonises the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway in clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma.
claims.source: and Notch has also been reported to antagonise the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway in clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma (Liu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Liu et al., 2013).

claims.claim: β-catenin activity levels are selected for by different types of cancer.
claims.source: The series of different Apc and Ctnnb1 mouse models that we employed have previously been used to show that β-catenin activity levels are selected for by different types of cancer, and these ectopic increases in signalling activity can also lead to a range of developmental defects (Kielman et al., 2002; Gaspar et al., 2009; Buchert et al., 2010; Bakker et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kielman et al., 2002; Gaspar et al., 2009; Buchert et al., 2010; Bakker et al., 2013).

claims.claim: LiCl, which is an inhibitor of GSK3β, can induce nephron formation but also blocks MET at high concentrations.
claims.source: It has been known for a long time that LiCl, which is an inhibitor of GSK3β, can induce nephron formation but it also blocks MET at high concentrations (Davies and Garrod, 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Davies and Garrod, 1995).

claims.claim: The PI3K pathway has been shown to alter Wnt signalling in embryonic stem cells.
claims.source: The significance of PI3K signalling in connection with Wnt/β-catenin pathway is strongly debated (Ng et al., 2009), but the PI3K pathway has not only been shown to alter Wnt signalling in the gut but also in embryonic stem cells (Paling et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Paling et al., 2004).

claims.claim: AKT phosphorylates β-catenin at Ser552.
claims.source: We tested whether β-catenin was phosphorylated at Ser552 as it has been reported to be by AKT (Fang et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Fang et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Proximal and medial nephron cells require Notch signalling and simultaneously need β-catenin and PI3K signalling to be kept at low levels, respectively.
claims.source: Together, these data show that proximal and medial nephron cells require Notch signalling and simultaneously need β-catenin and PI3K signalling to be kept at low levels, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments showing that reducing β-catenin or PI3K activity can partially rescue Notch inhibition phenotypes.

claims.claim: Changes in proliferation and apoptosis are not the driving force behind the β-catenin signalling gradient or the patterning of the nephron.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that changes in proliferation and apoptosis are not the driving force behind the β-catenin signalling gradient or the patterning of the nephron.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating proliferation or apoptosis does not affect nephron patterning.

claims.claim: Increasing and decreasing β-catenin signalling changes segmentation by forcing cells to change their identity.
claims.source: Together, these findings would therefore suggest that increasing and decreasing β-catenin signalling changes segmentation by forcing cells to change their identity and that this is the most likely mechanism underlying the alterations to segmentation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that β-catenin modulation affects segment identity without affecting proliferation or apoptosis.

claims.claim: The positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling.
claims.source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that BMP/PI3K pathway modulation affects β-catenin activity and nephron segmentation.

claims.claim: Simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling.
claims.source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that PI3K inhibition reduces β-catenin reporter activity.

claims.claim: Simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in increased β-catenin signalling.
claims.source: These data indicate that the positional identities in the nephron can be modified through BMP mediated PI3K/AKT signalling and that simulated increased BMP signalling (via inhibition of PI3K) leads to reduced β-catenin signalling, whereas simulated decreased BMP signalling (via inhibition of BMPR) results in the opposite effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that BMPR inhibition increases β-catenin reporter activity.

claims.claim: The observed phenotypes are due to a direct effect on the nephrogenic lineage rather than an indirect effect via the ureteric bud.
claims.source: To test if the observed phenotypes were due to a direct effect on the nephrogenic lineage or an indirect effect via the ureteric bud, we isolated metanephric mesenchyme away from the ureteric bud, induced it to form nephrons with spinal cord (Grobstein, 1953, 1955), and modulated β-catenin activity therein. Comparable to the phenotype observed in whole kidney rudiments, we found that inhibition of β-catenin activity favoured patterning towards the proximal fate, whereas increasing its activity had the opposite effect (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using isolated mesenchyme showing similar effects of β-catenin modulation as in whole kidneys, as shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The mechanism for the rescue of Notch inhibition phenotypes by β-catenin or PI3K inhibition is by reduction of the level of β-catenin signalling.
claims.source: In common to inhibition of β-catenin and PI3K was that they both decreased β-catenin signalling in nephrons and positively affected the development of the proximal-most and medial segments, respectively. Inhibition of β-catenin signalling in Notch-inhibited nephrons reduced the level of β-catenin signalling and rescued the proximal-most cells whilst co-inhibition of Notch and PI3K partially rescued the medial segment. It is therefore tempting to speculate that the mechanism for these rescues is by reduction of the level of β-catenin signalling.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation/inference from the observation that both β-catenin and PI3K inhibition reduce β-catenin signalling and rescue Notch inhibition phenotypes.

results.result: A β-catenin activity gradient exists along the proximal-distal axis of developing nephrons, with high activity distally and minimal activity in proximal podocytes. The gradient shows an exponential decrease (R²=0.999) with 15-72 fold differences between distal and proximal segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C8 provide converging evidence from TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP reporter quantification (C5, C6), confocal imaging (C7), and phospho-β-catenin antibody staining (C8). The exponential fit and quantitative measurements are well-documented in Figure 1, supporting the existence and characterization of the gradient.

results.result: Modulating β-catenin activity through pharmacological inhibitors causes dose-dependent shifts in nephron segment identities. Decreasing β-catenin promotes proximal identity and accelerates glomerular maturation, while increasing β-catenin expands distal segments and suppresses proximal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C13, C17-C20 demonstrate consistent effects of β-catenin modulation on nephron patterning using multiple approaches (time-lapse imaging, segment measurements, dose-response). The reversibility experiment (C13) and dose-dependent effects (C20) strengthen causality. Statistical significance is reported for key measurements.

results.result: Lgr5 expression in distal nephron segments increases with elevated β-catenin activity (3.0×, p=0.05), but Lgr5 homozygous mutants show no obvious kidney phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by Lgr5-EGFP reporter data and time-lapse quantification (Figure 3). However, the lack of phenotype in Lgr5 knockouts (C16) indicates Lgr5 is not functionally required for the patterning process, limiting the biological significance of the expression changes.

results.result: Mild β-catenin activation promotes distal segment gene expression (Wnt4, Pax8, Fgf8, Lhx1, Lgr5), and genetic models with elevated β-catenin (Apc+/1638N Ctnnb1+/E654) develop ectopic nephrons lacking proximal markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4D) and immunofluorescent analysis of genetic mutants (Figure 4F-G). The genetic validation strengthens the pharmacological findings, though the genetic models show variable penetrance and severity.

results.result: β-catenin-mediated nephron patterning occurs independently of changes in cell proliferation or apoptosis. Modulating β-catenin does not alter mitotic nuclei counts, and blocking proliferation with methotrexate does not affect segment marker expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25, C79 provide multiple lines of evidence excluding proliferation/apoptosis as mechanisms: H3(S10P) quantification shows no changes (C23), MTX-treated nephrons maintain correct patterning despite reduced size (C24), and TUNEL/Annexin V assays show minimal apoptosis (C25). The inference in C79 is well-supported by the data.

results.result: BMP signaling through PTEN/PI3K/AKT antagonizes β-catenin activity in the medial nephron segment. PI3K inhibition reduces β-catenin reporter activity and promotes medial segment development, while BMPR inhibition increases β-catenin activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C28-C32, C35-C36, C81-C83 demonstrate the BMP/PI3K/β-catenin interaction through multiple approaches: BRE-LacZ reporter (C28-C29), pPTEN/pAKT staining after inhibitor treatment (C30), TCF/Lef reporter quantification (C31-C32), and segment size measurements with qRT-PCR validation (C35-C36). The pathway logic is consistent with prior intestinal studies.

results.result: Co-inhibition of β-catenin or PI3K with Notch partially rescues proximal and medial segment identities normally lost by Notch inhibition alone, though Notch target gene expression is not restored.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40-C43, C78 demonstrate partial rescue of segment markers (Wt1, Podxl, LTL, Jag1) when β-catenin or PI3K inhibitors are combined with DAPT. However, C42 shows Notch target genes remain downregulated, and C85 acknowledges the mechanism is speculative. The rescue is partial and mechanistically incomplete, but the phenomenon is well-documented.

results.result: Simultaneous BMPR inhibition and β-catenin activation synergistically expands β-catenin signaling throughout nephrons, completely eliminating Wt1+ proximal cells and strongly reducing Jag1+ medial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by TCF/Lef::H2B-GFP reporter data and immunofluorescent staining showing very high β-catenin activity and loss of proximal/medial markers with dual treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-C). The synergistic effect is consistent with the proposed pathway interactions.

results.result: β-catenin phosphorylated at Ser552 localizes primarily to apical surfaces in distal and medial segments, with 80% of cells showing lateral/basal localization found in these segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are supported by immunofluorescent staining (Figure 6H) and quantitative cell counting. However, the functional significance is unclear as the phosphorylation pattern did not change with PI3K or BMPR inhibition (noted in text but not as a claim), limiting interpretation.

results.result: MET is only incompatible with very high levels of β-catenin activity, not moderate increases. Ectopic nephrons form at kidney periphery with increased β-catenin, are derived from Six2+ progenitors, and can be blocked by downstream inhibition with ICG001.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 provide dose-response data (Figure 4D, Figure 2—supplements 1-2), lineage tracing with Six2-CreGFP/Rosa26tdRFP (C48), and pathway specificity validation with ICG001 (C49) and alternative inhibitors BIO and salinomycin (C50-C51). The evidence establishes a dose-dependent relationship between β-catenin activity and MET competence.

results.result: The observed β-catenin modulation phenotypes result from direct effects on the nephrogenic lineage rather than indirect effects via the ureteric bud, as demonstrated by isolated mesenchyme experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by spinal cord-induced isolated mesenchyme experiments showing similar β-catenin modulation effects as whole kidneys (Figure 4E). This control experiment effectively excludes ureteric bud-mediated indirect effects, strengthening the interpretation of direct nephron patterning.

results.result: β-catenin signaling changes nephron segmentation by forcing cells to change their identity rather than through proliferation or apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is an inference supported by the combined evidence from proliferation/apoptosis experiments (C23-C25) and segment identity changes (C2, C11-C12, C17-C20). The logic is sound: since proliferation and apoptosis are unchanged, the segment size changes must result from cell fate specification changes.

results.result: Background knowledge claims from prior literature establishing the developmental context, pathway components, and precedents for gradient-based patterning in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C26-C27, C39, C52-C77 are citation-based claims establishing prior knowledge. These are appropriately cited and provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear accurate based on the referenced studies, though detailed verification of each citation is beyond the scope of this review.
